Family Health

Pelvic-floor exercises for men: when they help and how to start

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pelvic-floor muscle training, often called Kegel exercises, can help some men improve bladder control. It is commonly included in care after prostate surgery. The right programme depends on the problem: weakness, poor coordination and excessive muscle tension are not the same, and repeated strengthening is not the answer to every pelvic symptom.

Know what the muscles do

The pelvic floor is a group of muscles and supporting tissues at the base of the pelvis. It contributes to bladder and bowel control and sexual function. It is not just one muscle, and effective function requires both contraction and the ability to let go.

Ageing, some operations and other health problems can affect this system. Leakage is one possible sign of a problem, but difficulty urinating, pain or urgency can have several causes. A clinician can check whether exercise is appropriate before symptoms are attributed to weak muscles.

These exercises are named after Arnold Kegel, who described pelvic-floor training for urinary leakage in women in the 1940s. The same broad principle is used for different bodies, but pregnancy or childbirth-related problems and recovery after prostate surgery need different assessments. Youth does not guarantee a healthy pelvic floor, and ageing does not inevitably cause weakness.

Set realistic expectations

After radical prostatectomy, an appropriately taught programme can help some people regain continence sooner. It does not guarantee complete control or eliminate the possibility of other treatment. Follow the surgical team’s instructions about when to start or resume, particularly while a catheter is present.

Pelvic-floor training may help some aspects of sexual function, but it is not a universal cure for erection difficulties, early ejaculation or reduced orgasm intensity. These concerns can involve medicines, nerves, circulation, pain and emotional factors. Persistent problems deserve assessment rather than an ever more intensive exercise routine.

For women, supervised pelvic-floor training can help stress urinary leakage and some prolapse symptoms; sexual-function benefits vary. For men, bladder urgency may sometimes be addressed within a broader programme. Neither finding means that squeezing alone repairs every prolapse, prevents every early ejaculation or treats chronic prostatitis and pelvic pain.

Find a gentle inward lift

Imagine stopping the passage of gas and gently lifting the muscles inward. Some men notice a small lift around the base of the penis or scrotum. Keep the buttocks and thighs relaxed and breathe normally. The movement should be an inward squeeze rather than pushing down.

Practise away from the toilet. Repeatedly stopping urine midstream is not a training method and can interfere with emptying the bladder. If you cannot identify the action, a pelvic-health physiotherapist or continence clinician can check the technique and, when useful, offer feedback tools.

Use a programme matched to your capacity

Start with a comfortable contraction that you can release fully. A clinician may use a brief hold of a few seconds initially, followed by enough rest, and adjust repetitions as control improves. Longer holds and quick contractions can serve different purposes, but neither should cause pain or straining.

Long holds and high repetition counts are not a safe universal target. Quality, breathing and relaxation are more important than a maximum number. Training can be practised lying, sitting or standing as advised; you do not need to keep the muscles clenched throughout the day.

For a person advised to strengthen, NIDDK describes an initial squeeze of about three seconds followed by full release, gradually working toward ten to fifteen repetitions as appropriate. This is an example to adapt with the clinician, not a requirement to hold for twenty seconds or repeat twenty squeezes four times daily. Avoid tightening the abdomen and do not hold your breath.

Do not strengthen through pain

Pelvic pain, painful ejaculation, urinary hesitancy or difficulty relaxing may occur when muscles are overactive or tender. A pelvic-floor assessment may point toward relaxation, coordination work or another treatment rather than repeated squeezing. More effort can be counterproductive when the muscles already struggle to release.

Stop and seek advice if exercises trigger pain, worsen leakage or make bladder or bowel emptying harder. Inability to pass urine with a painful full bladder needs urgent care. Blood in the urine, fever or a new significant symptom also needs medical assessment rather than exercise alone.

Review progress with the clinician

Improvement usually takes repeated practice over weeks, and recovery after surgery may take longer. Keep a simple record of symptoms and the prescribed routine. If there is no progress, review the technique and diagnosis rather than assuming you have failed or should double the workload.

Treatment may combine exercise with bladder training, medicines or other continence options according to the cause. Discuss sexual symptoms openly as well. A tailored plan aims to improve function and comfort, not to make the pelvic floor permanently tight or promise a particular sexual performance.

Basic practice needs no purchased equipment and can fit into ordinary routines. Professional assessment may still be important, particularly after surgery or when symptoms are painful. Low cost does not mean an exercise is risk-free or suitable for every diagnosis.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NIDDK advises correct muscle identification, complete relaxation and an individual programme without overtraining or routine midstream practice.

AUA guidance supports training in selected post-prostate-treatment care and assessment of muscle pain or overactivity before strengthening.

How BeMama can help

Ask someone trained in pelvic health to check both the squeeze and release, then review symptoms rather than chasing higher counts.

When to seek help

Stop exercises that cause pain or worsen emptying; acute inability to pass urine needs urgent care.

Sources and further reading

  • NIDDK — NIDDK: Kegel exercises
  • AUA — AUA: incontinence after prostate treatment, amended 2024
  • AUA — AUA: male chronic pelvic pain guideline, 2025

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Both contraction and relaxation are essential.
  • Do not routinely practise by stopping urine midstream.
  • Pain or difficulty emptying calls for assessment, not harder squeezing.

Frequently asked questions

Are Kegels a guaranteed treatment for erectile dysfunction?

No. They may help selected people, but erection difficulties have several possible causes and may need other treatment.

Should I increase repetitions if I get pelvic pain?

No. Stop and ask for assessment; excessive tension may require a different approach.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
